text: Given an array nums and a value val, remove every occurrence of val in place. Let k be the number of elements not equal to val. Put those elements into the first k positions and return k. Their order can change, and the rest of the array doesn't matter.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — in place means constant extra space. I return the count k, the first k entries must be the elements that aren't val, and anything past k is don't-care. Is that right?
Exactly. The order among the kept elements is flexible.

Let me run through the example. Three, two, two, three, with val equal to three. Both threes go away, so k is two, and the first two entries are two, two. Whatever sits past them doesn't matter. That matches.

Let me think. A naive approach would literally delete each val with erase. But every erase shifts everything after it, so the whole thing becomes quadratic time. This problem reminds me of the slow and fast two-pointer pattern, because what I really need is an in-place filter. A fast pointer reads every element; a slow write pointer, i, marks where the next kept element goes. When the value isn't val, I write it at i and move i forward. When it is val, I skip it and leave i alone. At the end, everything from zero up to i is a kept element, and i is k.
Is it safe to overwrite the same array while you're reading it?

Yes, because the write pointer never passes the read pointer. i only moves on a keep, so i is always at most the read index. Every write lands on a slot I've already read, or on the current one, writing it back to itself. It never overwrites data I haven't reached yet, so no extra buffer is needed.

Here's the plan. One: start the write pointer i at zero. Two: read each number; if it equals val, skip it and leave i where it is; otherwise write it at i and move i forward. Three: return i, which is k. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one range-for loop with a write pointer. If num equals val, I continue; otherwise I write num at i plus plus. Then I return i. One thing worth flagging — that write line does two jobs: it writes at i, then the post-increment moves i forward. The skip branch must not touch i. If i moved on a skip too, the two pointers would move together, and val would stay inside the first k. This is linear time, constant space, and it keeps the order of the kept elements.

Yes — if val is rare, a swap-with-end version writes less. When nums at i equals val, I copy the last element over it and shrink the effective length. Only the val positions get written, and kept elements never move. The catch is that I must not advance i after that swap — the element pulled from the end hasn't been checked and might itself be val, so I re-check it in place. The trade-off: swap writes once per val but reorders the array, while my overwrite version does up to n writes but keeps the order. Since order is flexible here, either is fine; I'd default to the overwrite one for clarity.

Let's dry-run the code. Zero, one, three, zero, two, with val equal to zero. The row that matters is the second zero: it's skipped, so i stays at two while the read pointer moves on. That's how the gap closes — the final two lands in slot two, not slot four. It returns k equals three, and the first three are one, three, two — all the non-zero elements, in order. Corner cases: three, two, two, three with val three gives two; an empty array gives zero; an array that's all val gives zero. I also ran it on five thousand random arrays, checking that the first k are exactly the non-val elements — zero failures.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, constant work per element. Space is constant — just the write pointer. The most writes happen when nothing equals val: every element is written once, back onto itself. Oh, one more thing — this write-pointer skeleton generalizes directly. Swap the keep condition, num not equal to val, for something else and you get a whole family. Deduplicating a sorted array is keep if different from the last kept. Pushing zeros to the back is keep if non-zero, then pad the tail with zeros. It's really an in-place filter — the same thing standard remove if does under the hood.

Clean. Three things stood out. You avoided the erase trap instead of deleting element by element. You explained why overwriting in place is safe, because the write pointer never passes the read pointer. And you knew the swap variant's re-check subtlety, plus when each version is the better pick. Nice.
